slides.title: Percolation on networks: site, bond + critical thresholds
slides.body:
**Percolation theory** asks: when does a giant connected cluster appear in a randomly damaged or constructed network? Originally a physics question (Broadbent + Hammersley 1957) about flow through porous media. Now central to network science — failures, immunization, robustness, epidemics, phase transitions.

**Site percolation**: each node is **present** with probability p, **absent** with probability 1 - p. Ask: for which p does a **giant cluster** spanning the network exist?

**Bond percolation**: each edge is **present** with probability p, absent with probability 1 - p. Equivalent to site percolation in some settings; subtly different in general.

**Critical threshold p_c** = smallest p at which a giant cluster exists. Below p_c: cluster sizes O(log n) or smaller. Above p_c: a unique giant cluster of size O(n).

**Lattice + regular networks**: p_c is geometry-dependent.
- 2D square lattice bond: p_c = 1/2 (Kesten 1980).
- 2D triangular lattice site: p_c = 1/2.
- Bethe lattice (tree) with branching b: p_c = 1/(b-1).
- 3D simple cubic bond: p_c ≈ 0.2488.

**Erdős-Rényi**: bond percolation on G(n, p̃) — equivalent to G(n, p·p̃), so p_c·⟨k⟩ = 1, i.e. p_c = 1/⟨k⟩.

**General networks (Molloy + Reed 1995; Cohen + Erez + ben-Avraham + Havlin 2000)**:
  **Molloy-Reed criterion**: giant component exists iff ⟨k²⟩ - 2⟨k⟩ > 0, i.e. **⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩ > 2**.
  Equivalent **percolation threshold**: p_c = ⟨k⟩ / (⟨k²⟩ - ⟨k⟩).

**Scale-free networks** (Cohen + Erez + ben-Avraham + Havlin 2000): for P(k) ~ k^(-γ), ⟨k²⟩ diverges when γ ≤ 3. Then **p_c → 0** in the thermodynamic limit — scale-free networks **always** have a giant component regardless of how much you damage them randomly. Foundational for understanding Internet robustness.

**Robustness vs attack** (Albert + Jeong + Barabási 2000 Nature *Error + attack tolerance of complex networks*):
- **Random failure**: scale-free networks extraordinarily robust (most random removals hit low-degree nodes that barely matter).
- **Targeted attack** (remove highest-degree hubs first): scale-free networks shatter rapidly; random networks more uniform under both regimes.
- **Mixed strategies**: real networks face combination.

**Continuous vs discontinuous percolation** (Achlioptas + D'Souza + Spencer 2009 Science): rules that delay or accelerate cluster merging can shift the transition from continuous (2nd-order) to abrupt (1st-order). 'Explosive percolation' studied intensively 2010s.

**Algorithms**:
- **Newman-Ziff cluster-growth**: efficient simulation.
- **Union-Find data structures** + path compression.
- **Generating-function approach** (Newman + Strogatz + Watts 2001): analytical for arbitrary degree distributions.

slides.title: Epidemics on networks: SIR/SIS + targeted immunization
slides.body:
**Epidemic models** describe disease (or rumor, behavior) spread.

**SIR (Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered)** + **SIS (Susceptible-Infectious-Susceptible)** are canonical compartmental models.
- **SIR**: S + I → 2I at rate β per S-I edge; I → R at rate γ. R immune.
- **SIS**: S + I → 2I at rate β; I → S at rate γ. No permanent immunity.

**Mass-action (well-mixed) basic reproduction number**: R_0 = β/γ × ⟨k⟩ (rough). Threshold R_0 > 1 for outbreak; below 1 disease dies out.

**On networks** the picture changes radically. Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani (2001 PRL *Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks*) derived:

  **Epidemic threshold λ_c = ⟨k⟩ / ⟨k²⟩**

for SIS on uncorrelated networks via heterogeneous mean-field theory. **For scale-free networks with γ ≤ 3, ⟨k²⟩ diverges → λ_c → 0** — diseases always spread, no matter how small β/γ. Foundational result; explained HIV/AIDS spread on heavy-tailed sexual contact networks (Liljeros 2001).

**Critical implications**:
- **Vaccinate randomly**: useless on scale-free networks (random nodes are low-degree).
- **Vaccinate highest-degree hubs (targeted)** (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2002): efficient; restores finite threshold.
- **Acquaintance immunization** (Cohen + Havlin + ben-Avraham 2003): pick random nodes + immunize a random *friend* of theirs (exploits friendship paradox — your friends have higher degree than you on average). Easy to deploy when degrees aren't known.
- **Ring vaccination**: vaccinate contacts of confirmed cases (smallpox, Ebola).

**Refinements**:
- **Heterogeneous degree-block mean-field**: separate ODEs per degree class.
- **Pair approximation** + **moment-closure**: capture correlations.
- **Discrete-time + stochastic agent-based**: simulation-driven (FluTE, GleamViz, EpiSimS, CovaSim).
- **Networked SEIR + COVID models** (Vespignani's MOBS lab; Imperial College Ferguson 2020; Stanford Lessler).
- **Annealed vs quenched** networks: quenched (fixed topology) shows lower thresholds + heterogeneous outbreak sizes.

**Spectral approach** (Wang + Chakrabarti + Wang + Faloutsos 2003; Castellano + Pastor-Satorras 2010): epidemic threshold on **any** network is λ_c = 1/Λ_max(A) where Λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix. For scale-free networks Λ_max ~ √k_max → divergent.

**Vespignani group COVID-19 work**: networked metapopulation models with global airline + commuting data informed pandemic policy. Pastor-Satorras + Castellano + Van Mieghem + Vespignani 2015 *Reviews of Modern Physics* is the canonical review.

**Bond percolation = SIR equivalence** (Newman 2002 PRE): the final size of an SIR outbreak with transmissibility T = β/(β+γ) per edge equals the giant cluster of bond percolation at p = T. Gives analytical exact final-size distribution.

**Immunization strategies summary**:
- Random: poor on heterogeneous networks.
- Targeted by degree: highly effective.
- Acquaintance: practical when degrees unknown.
- Ring vaccination: when only cases known.
- Network-informed (digital contact tracing, mobility data): COVID-era + future.

slides.title: Cascades + threshold models: complex contagion
slides.body:
**Simple vs complex contagion** (Centola + Macy 2007 American Journal of Sociology):
- **Simple contagion** (SIR-like): each infectious contact independently transmits with probability β. One contact may suffice — like flu.
- **Complex contagion**: adoption requires **multiple reinforcing contacts**. Threshold-based — like behaviors, opinions, joining a movement, technology adoption.

**Granovetter threshold model** (1978 American Journal of Sociology *Threshold models of collective behavior*): each agent i has threshold θ_i. Agent adopts (riots, joins protest) iff the fraction of adopted neighbors ≥ θ_i. Heterogeneous θ_i across agents produces **cascades + tipping points**. Tiny threshold differences can determine whether a movement succeeds or stalls. Foundational sociology paper; informed marketing, viral diffusion, political mobilization.

**Watts cascade model** (2002 PNAS *Simple model of global cascades on random networks*): linear-threshold model on networks. Each node activates if its fraction of active neighbors ≥ θ. Watts showed:
- **Cascade window**: cascades only occur for certain combinations of ⟨k⟩ + θ.
- **Vulnerability**: nodes with k_i < 1/θ are 'vulnerable' (a single neighbor can flip them).
- **Global cascade condition**: requires a connected component of vulnerable nodes (a 'vulnerable cluster') that percolates.
- Low ⟨k⟩: graph too sparse, cascade fizzles.
- High ⟨k⟩: most nodes need many active neighbors → cascade fails.
- Sweet spot in between → cascade window.

**Centola 2010 *The Spread of Behavior in an Online Social Network Experiment* (Science)**: ran a randomized experiment on an online health-behavior platform. **Clustered** (lattice-like) networks spread behavior **faster** than random networks for complex contagion — opposite of simple contagion. Mechanism: clustered networks provide multiple-reinforcement signals; random networks don't. Important applied result.

**Long ties + the strength of weak ties**: Granovetter (1973) showed weak ties (acquaintances) carry novel information. But for complex contagion (Centola), strong ties + clustered networks matter more — adoption needs social reinforcement, not just exposure.

**Influence maximization** (Kempe + Kleinberg + Tardos 2003 KDD): given a network + threshold/cascade model, find k seed nodes that maximize expected adoption. NP-hard but **submodular** → greedy 1 - 1/e approximation. Foundation of viral-marketing literature. Many extensions (CELF heuristic, IMM, RIS).

**Independent cascade model**: each newly-active node tries each neighbor once with probability p_ij; if success, neighbor becomes active. Closely related to bond percolation.

**Real-world cascades**:
- **Twitter retweet cascades** (Goel + Watts + Goldstein 2012): mostly shallow + small; rare deep cascades are 'broadcast-like' from a single hub, not viral.
- **Hashtag adoption** (Romero + Meeder + Kleinberg 2011): political hashtags require multiple exposures; mundane hashtags spread like simple contagion.
- **Financial cascades**: bank-failure contagion (Battiston 2012 DebtRank, COVID supply chain shocks 2020).
- **Power grid cascades** (Buldyrev + Parshani + Paul + Stanley + Havlin 2010 Nature) on interdependent networks: cascading failures across coupled networks (power grid + Internet) → catastrophic. Studied intensively after 2003 + 2012 blackouts.
- **Bootstrap percolation**: similar to threshold model; nodes activate when k ≥ θ neighbors active.

**Modern + open**: cascade prediction (deepRetweet, CasFlow, GNN models); influence maximization at scale; reverse engineering 'seeds' from observed cascades; identifying super-spreaders in disease + behavior; manipulating cascades in misinformation contexts.

question.question: Derive epidemic threshold λ_c on uncorrelated network
question.goal: Show λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ for SIS via heterogeneous mean-field (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001).

steps.prompt: Define ρ_k = fraction of infected among nodes of degree k. What's the probability a random neighbor is infected? Use friendship-paradox: probability your neighbor has degree k is proportional to k·P(k)/⟨k⟩.
hints: Edge points to node of degree k with prob k P(k)/⟨k⟩.
steps.reveal: Probability a random edge ends at infected node = Θ = (1/⟨k⟩) Σ_k k P(k) ρ_k. (Friendship-paradox weighting: higher-degree nodes more likely to be at end of random edge.)

steps.prompt: Write the rate equation for ρ_k under SIS dynamics: rate in = (1-ρ_k) · k · λ · Θ; rate out = ρ_k.
steps.motivation: Healing rate normalized to 1; infection rate λ = β/γ per S-I edge.
hints: Susceptible fraction (1-ρ_k) infected at rate λk·Θ; recover at rate 1.
steps.reveal: dρ_k/dt = -ρ_k + λ·k·(1 - ρ_k)·Θ. At steady state: ρ_k = λ·k·Θ / (1 + λ·k·Θ).

steps.prompt: Substitute steady-state ρ_k into Θ + linearize near Θ = 0 to find threshold.

acceptedAnswers: Θ ≈ (λ/⟨k⟩) Σ_k k² P(k) Θ = λ ⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩ · Θ

steps.reveal: Near Θ → 0: ρ_k ≈ λ·k·Θ. Then Θ = (1/⟨k⟩) Σ_k k·P(k)·(λ·k·Θ) = (λ·⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩)·Θ. Nontrivial solution requires λ·⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩ ≥ 1.

**λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩**. For scale-free networks with γ ≤ 3, ⟨k²⟩ diverges (in the n → ∞ limit) → λ_c → 0. Diseases always spread regardless of infection rate. Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001 PRL; canonical result. Explains why heavy-tailed sexual networks (Liljeros 2001) facilitate HIV spread + why targeted immunization (removing hubs) restores a finite threshold.

question.question: Why is targeted (hub-based) immunization dramatically more effective than random immunization on scale-free networks?
options: On scale-free networks with P(k) ~ k^(-γ), γ ≤ 3, the epidemic threshold λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ → 0 (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001 PRL) because ⟨k²⟩ diverges. Random immunization removes nodes uniformly — most random picks are low-degree leaves that barely matter for transmission; the few hubs remain. Targeted immunization (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2002): rank by degree + remove highest first; removing the top ~5-10% of hubs typically shatters the giant component + restores a finite threshold. **Acquaintance immunization** (Cohen + Havlin + ben-Avraham 2003 PRL): when degrees are unknown, pick a random node + immunize a random friend (exploits the **friendship paradox** — your friends have higher expected degree than you, k_friend ≈ ⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩); also highly effective + practical. Modern variants: contact-tracing networks; ring vaccination (smallpox, Ebola); mobility-based targeting in COVID-19 (Vespignani MOBS lab). The asymmetry mirrors Albert + Jeong + Barabási (2000 Nature) error/attack tolerance: scale-free networks robust to random failure + fragile to targeted attack. Both follow from the heavy tail.
question.explanation: On scale-free networks λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ → 0 (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001) since ⟨k²⟩ diverges. Random immunization misses hubs (mostly hits leaves). Targeted by degree (PS+V 2002): remove top 5-10% hubs to restore finite threshold. Acquaintance immunization (Cohen + Havlin + ben-Avraham 2003): immunize random friend of random node — exploits friendship paradox. Mirrors error/attack tolerance asymmetry (Albert + Jeong + Barabási 2000).

slides.workedSolution: On scale-free networks λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ → 0 since ⟨k²⟩ diverges (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001). Targeted immunization of top-degree hubs shatters giant component + restores finite threshold. Acquaintance immunization (Cohen + Havlin + ben-Avraham 2003) exploits friendship paradox when degrees unknown. Mirrors Albert + Jeong + Barabási 2000 robustness/fragility asymmetry.

question.question: A novel respiratory pathogen is spreading in a country with heavy-tailed contact network (γ ≈ 2.5).
question.prompt: You have 10% vaccine doses available. Compare expected outcomes for: (a) uniform random allocation, (b) age-targeted (elderly first), (c) hub-targeted via mobility + contact-tracing data, (d) acquaintance-based (vaccinate friend of random sample). Quantify expected reduction in final outbreak size using percolation theory + epidemic threshold ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩. What ethical + practical considerations make pure hub-targeted infeasible? How would you integrate genomic + mobility data à la COVID era (Vespignani MOBS, GISAID)?

question.question: Write the heterogeneous-mean-field epidemic threshold λ_c for SIS on an uncorrelated network with degree distribution P(k).

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how network structure controls spreading + percolation.
question.rubric: Mentions: Percolation threshold (Molloy + Reed 1995; Cohen + Erez + ben-Avraham + Havlin 2000) p_c = ⟨k⟩/(⟨k²⟩ - ⟨k⟩); for scale-free networks with γ ≤ 3, ⟨k²⟩ diverges + p_c → 0 — networks always have giant component. Epidemic threshold (Pastor-Satorras + Vespignani 2001) λ_c = ⟨k⟩/⟨k²⟩ vanishes similarly; diseases always spread on heterogeneous networks. Explains HIV spread on heavy-tailed sexual networks (Liljeros 2001). Spectral form λ_c = 1/Λ_max(A). Targeted hub immunization (PS+V 2002) restores finite threshold; acquaintance immunization (Cohen + Havlin + ben-Avraham 2003) exploits friendship paradox. SIR = bond percolation (Newman 2002). Cascades: Granovetter (1978) thresholds; Watts (2002) cascade window; Centola (2010) showed complex contagion spreads faster on clustered networks. Influence maximization (Kempe + Kleinberg + Tardos 2003) submodular → greedy 1 - 1/e. Real-world: COVID-19 (Vespignani MOBS), Buldyrev 2010 cascading failures on interdependent networks.
